items.stem: Explain how changes in agriculture helped the Industrial Revolution.
items.answer: New methods (crop rotation, seed drill, selective breeding) and enclosure produced more food to feed growing towns, and fewer farm workers were needed, so labour moved to factories; farmers’ profits could also be invested.
items.markingKey: 1 mark food supply; 1 mark labour released; 1 mark capital [3]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that the supply of coal was the most important reason why Britain was the first country to industrialise. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: Coal fuelled steam engines and, as coke, smelted iron (Darby, 1709). Britain’s coalfields were large and close to iron ore and ports. Disagree: Agricultural change fed the towns and released labour. Capital from trade and banking paid for factories and canals. Population growth supplied workers and customers; the empire supplied cotton and markets. Judgement: Coal was essential, but it mattered because it combined with capital, labour and markets; together they explain Britain’s lead.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

A single privy serves a whole court of families, and the river is a black stream full of rubbish and filth.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Suggest the purpose of Source C. Explain your answer. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of living conditions in Manchester that Source C does not show.
items.answer: (a) To expose the poverty created by industry and criticise the factory owners and the system. (b) How wealthier areas of Manchester looked, or the death rates in the town.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: A student investigating working conditions for children in the 1830s finds Source C. Source C: evidence given by a former child mill worker to the Sadler Committee, 1832 (adapted). “At busy times we worked from three in the morning until ten at night. When I was too tired the overlooker strapped me. I was made crooked by the work and now cannot walk without crutches.” (a) Explain one reason why Source C may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of conditions for child workers that Source C does not show.
items.answer: (a) May be reliable: it is first-hand testimony from someone who worked in a mill, given at the time. May not be reliable: Sadler wanted a Ten Hours law and chose witnesses who supported his case; the committee did not hear mill owners before reporting. (b) Whether conditions were the same in all mills, or what owners said in reply.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Put these events in chronological order, starting with the earliest. A: The Ten Hours Act limited women and young people to ten hours a day in textile mills. B: The Trades Union Congress (TUC) was founded. C: The People’s Charter was published. D: The Factory Act banned children under 9 from working in textile mills.
items.markingKey: Correct order D, C, A, B (D 1833; C 1838; A 1847; B 1868). 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if one adjacent pair is reversed. [2]

items.stem: Explain why many factory owners opposed factory reform.
items.answer: They feared shorter hours would cut output and profits, make British goods less competitive and that the government should not interfere in business (laissez-faire).
items.markingKey: 1 mark profits/competition; 1 mark laissez-faire [2]

items.stem: A student investigating the aims and failure of Chartism finds Source A. Source A: the People’s Charter, 1838 (adapted summary of its six points). “A vote for every man twenty-one years of age; the secret ballot; no property qualification for Members of Parliament; payment of Members; equal electoral districts; annual parliaments.” Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: To set out the movement’s demands clearly so that people would sign the petitions to Parliament.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: Source C is taken from the People’s Charter, 1838 (adapted summary of its six points). It says: “A vote for every man twenty-one years of age; the secret ballot; no property qualification for Members of Parliament; payment of Members; equal electoral districts; annual parliaments.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Is Source C a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of what the Chartists wanted that Source C does not show.
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) That women were not included, or that the petitions of 1839, 1842 and 1848 were rejected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “money and wealth available to invest in new businesses, machines and buildings”.
items.answer: Capital
items.markingKey: Capital: money and wealth available to invest in new businesses, machines and buildings. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “The Industrial Revolution happened suddenly in the year 1800.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It was a gradual process from about 1750 to 1850, building on earlier changes in farming, trade and technology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how trade and the empire helped to provide capital for industry.
items.answer: Merchants made large profits from overseas trade (sugar, tobacco, cotton, enslaved people) and banks lent money, so there was capital to invest in factories, canals and machines. Colonies also supplied raw cotton and markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark profits/capital; 1 mark banks/investment; 1 mark raw materials/markets [3]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “Where the open fields have been enclosed, the land produces twice as much corn. The farmers are richer and the rents higher, though the cottager has lost his cow and his common.” (A report on farming written by the agricultural writer Arthur Young in 1771 (adapted).) What can you infer from Source A about the effects of enclosure?
items.answer: Enclosure increased output and profits for farmers and landowners but harmed poorer cottagers who lost common rights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: The table shows the approximate populations of two industrial towns. Glasgow: 1801 about 77 000  1851 about 329 000. Liverpool: 1801 about 78 000  1851 about 376 000. (a) Calculate the increase in the population of Glasgow between 1801 and 1851. (b) Which town grew faster in percentage terms?
items.answer: (a) 252 000 (b) Liverpool (382% compared with 327%)

items.stem: “The supply of coal was the most important reason why Britain was the first country to industrialise.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: population growth; capital and trade.
items.answer: Agree: Coal fuelled steam engines and, as coke, smelted iron (Darby, 1709). Britain’s coalfields were large and close to iron ore and ports. Disagree: Agricultural change fed the towns and released labour. Capital from trade and banking paid for factories and canals. Population growth supplied workers and customers; the empire supplied cotton and markets. Judgement: Coal was essential, but it mattered because it combined with capital, labour and markets; together they explain Britain’s lead.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a hand-powered machine invented by James Hargreaves that spun several threads at once”.
items.answer: Spinning jenny
items.markingKey: Spinning jenny: a hand-powered machine invented by James Hargreaves that spun several threads at once. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “The first factories were powered by water rather than steam.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Early mills such as Arkwright’s Cromford Mill (1771) used water wheels.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A student investigating how the factory system changed work finds Source B. Source B: a description of a cotton mill by a visitor to Manchester, 1835 (adapted). “Hundreds of spinning machines turn in a single room, driven by one great steam engine below. The noise is so great that the workers speak by signs, and the overlookers walk the rows to see that no machine stands idle.” Is Source B a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer.
items.answer: Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2]

items.stem: The table shows the approximate length of railway in Britain: 1830 – 100 miles, 1840 – 1 500 miles, 1850 – 6 000 miles, 1860 – 10 400 miles, 1870 – 13 600 miles. (a) A journey of 300 km took a stagecoach averaging 12 km/h and a train averaging 40 km/h. Calculate how many hours were saved by train. (b) Suggest one group of people who might have opposed the railways, and why.
items.answer: (a) 17.5 hours (b) Canal and stagecoach owners (lost business) or landowners (lines crossed their estates).
items.markingKey: (a) 300/12 = 25 h; 300/40 = 7.5 h; saving 17.5 h [2] (b) 1 mark group; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A student investigating the impact of railways in the 1830s and 1840s finds Source A. Source A: a newspaper report on the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, September 1830 (adapted). “The engines drew carriages filled with passengers at a speed of more than twenty miles an hour. The whole route was lined with crowds who had come to see this wonder of the age.” (a) What can you infer from Source A about attitudes to the early railways? (b) Explain one reason why Source A may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) The railway was seen as an exciting new wonder and attracted huge public interest. (b) May be reliable: it was written at the time of the event by a reporter who was there. May not be reliable: the reporter may have exaggerated the excitement to make a good story; it does not mention the accident that killed the MP William Huskisson on the opening day.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “cholera”?
options: An outdoor toilet, often shared by many households and emptied rarely.
A disease spread by lice that thrived in crowded, dirty housing.
A water-borne disease spread by sewage-contaminated water, which killed tens of thousands in British epidemics in 1831-32 and 1848-49.
Cheap terraced houses built sharing a back wall, with no back yard and little ventilation.
items.answer: A water-borne disease spread by sewage-contaminated water, which killed tens of thousands in British epidemics in 1831-32 and 1848-49.
items.markingKey: Cholera: a water-borne disease spread by sewage-contaminated water, which killed tens of thousands in British epidemics in 1831-32 and 1848-49. [1]

items.stem: Explain why factory owners employed so many children.
items.answer: Children were cheap (paid much less than adults), small enough to crawl under machines and easy to discipline; families needed the extra income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cheap; 1 mark size/obedience; 1 mark family need [3]

items.stem: Chadwick’s 1842 report gave the average age of death by social group. Liverpool: professional persons and gentry 35, tradesmen 22, labourers 15. Rutland (a rural county): gentry 52, farmers and tradesmen 41, labourers 38. Explain one limitation of using this data alone to judge living conditions.
items.answer: Averages hide the range (many died as babies while some lived long lives); figures cover only some places and Chadwick wanted to prove the case for reform.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Source D is taken from a book defending factories written by Andrew Ure, 1835 (adapted). It says: “I have visited many factories and never saw a child punished. The children seemed always cheerful and active, taking pleasure in the light play of their muscles.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Is Source D a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) Suggest the purpose of Source D. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) To defend the factory system and argue against reform.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: A student investigating living conditions in industrial towns finds Source A. Source A: Friedrich Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England, 1845 (adapted). “In the old town of Manchester the houses are filthy and crowded together. A single privy serves a whole court of families, and the river is a black stream full of rubbish and filth.” (a) What can you infer from Source A about living conditions in Manchester? (b) Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer. (c) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of living conditions in Manchester that Source A does not show.
items.answer: (a) Living conditions were overcrowded and unsanitary, with very few toilets and a heavily polluted river. (b) To expose the poverty created by industry and criticise the factory owners and the system. (c) How wealthier areas of Manchester looked, or the death rates in the town.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (c) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “The 1833 Factory Act ended child labour in Britain.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It banned only under-9s from textile mills and limited hours for older children; it did not cover mines or other industries, and enforcement was weak.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the importance of the Tolpuddle Martyrs to the trade union movement.
items.answer: Their harsh sentence caused a huge public protest and petition, leading to their pardon in 1836; they became a symbol of workers’ rights to organise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark protest/pardon; 1 mark symbol [2]

items.stem: Before 1833 a 12-year-old child in a cotton mill worked 13 hours a day, 6 days a week. The 1833 Factory Act limited children aged 9 to 13 to 9 hours a day (and no more than 48 hours a week). Calculate the percentage reduction in weekly hours if the child worked the maximum 48 hours.

“The Factory Acts quickly improved life for working children.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: inspectors and enforcement; industries covered; later Acts.
items.answer: Agree: The 1833 Act banned under-9s from textile mills and limited hours; the 1847 Ten Hours Act reduced hours further. Inspectors made enforcement possible for the first time. Disagree: There were only four inspectors in 1833 and ages were hard to prove. Mines were not covered until 1842 and many other trades much later. Children still worked long hours in workshops and at home. Judgement: The Acts were an important start, but improvement was slow and uneven; real change came over several decades.
